Messages.Author: Jay Kristoff
Messages.Body:
Here is the new game win rule:
3.8.1. Game Win Scoring

A player receives a Game Win at the end of a game in which they have
received at least two (2) Victory Points and have more Victory Points than
any other player in the game. (No game win is awarded in the case of ties.)

In the case of a 2-2-1 tie no game win is awarded, but everyone is
credited with their VPs. As for losses, who's keeping track of that anyway?
Next year the criteria for final round seating will be: game wins, victory
points, and tournament points; in that order. Not every table will have a
game win. That should mean that VPs will still be quite important.
Jay

>>In the case of a 2-2-1 tie no game win is awarded, but everyone is
credited with their VPs.>>

I managed to go find the actual rule about ties at some point (teach me to ask
questions before I go lookat the rules :-). I'd think that it'd be a good idea
to make a tie for first worth more than a loss (i.e. if you split a table 2/2,
you have preference over someone who who doesn't, but the VPs might make it
work that way anyways), but I don't think it is gonna be that important.

I'd also think that playing at a 4 player table would be less optimal in this
setting--more likely to tie, but that also might be rather insignificant.

>>As for losses, who's keeping track of that anyway?>>

Well, someone will--you play three games and win 1 of them, you have 2 losses
:-)

>>Next year the criteria for final round seating will be: game wins, victory
points, and tournament points; in that order. Not every table will have a
game win. That should mean that VPs will still be quite important.>>

Yup. Where I see this being problematic, however, is in the obvious
situation--a guy who accidentally wins one table with a 2-1-1-1 point split but
gets no other VPs during the rest of the tournament will get into the finals
way before the guy who never actually wins a table, but gets 2 VPs in each
round (point splitting each table 3-2). Guy A has 2 VPs where guy B has 6, but
guy A gets into the finals before guy B, which is kind of wonky. I guess it no
longer pays to play an intercept deck.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Jeroen wrote:
>>I was thinking just the opposite. If an intercept can oust 1 prey and be
the last one standing, (wich is IMO not so difficult for such a deck) it
does have a game win.>>

Most reliable intercept decks I have seen rarely can oust their first prey (too
much defense, which is necessary if you want to be a reliable intercept
deck)--they get 2 VPs by virtue of being the last guy standing (1 VP for
ousting the other player left in the game and 1 VP for being the last guy
alive), and the player who was originally his prey generally has the other
three.

The only intercept decks I have seen that can reliably oust their prey are
Smiling Jack based decks, and they are difficult to pull off, as you suddenly
need to fend off the whole table (you probably need a huge vampire and, like,
30 Obediances...)

Peter,
I don't think this will ever be a problem. I don't know about big national
tournaments but a local one for us would go something like this:
players are:
1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8.

First game:
1,2,3,4----Player 1 gets 3VP player 3 gets 1VP(table win player 1)
5,6,7,8----Player 5 gets 4VP(table win player 5)

Second game :
7,1,8,2----Player 1 gets 3VP player 2 gets 1VP(table win player 1)
3,5,4,6----Player 5 gets 2 VP player 3 gets 2 VP(tie, no table win)

Third Game:
4,7,6,1----Player 6 gets 3 VP player 7 gets 1 VP
8,3,2,5----Some how Player 8(Peter Bakija) "accidently gets 2VP, player 5
gets 1, 2 gets 1(table win to 8)

Totals:
1-6(2)
2-2
3-3
4-
5-7(1)
6-3(1)
7-1
8-2(1)

Players in the finals via table points are: 1,3,5,6,8
Players in the finals via Victory points are: 1,3,5,6, with a tie breaker
between 8 and 2.
Only difference, no tie breaker. Much better in my opinion. As the
tournament gets larger the chance of someone with only 1 table win going
anywhere on a fluke(IE not having a ton of VP to break table win-ties) goes
way down. This is pretty much what I can remember from our last tournament.
The same people getting into the finals from VP would have been the same
people into the finals from table wins, except the last spot which was a VP
tie.

Basically, it puts more importance on being able to run the table once, then
perform standard over multiple rounds.(difference between getting 1-1-2 VP
in a tournament and 0-0-4)
--

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
pd...@aol.comANTISPAM (Peter D Bakija) wrote in message news:<20011028161414...@mb-cp.aol.com>...

> I managed to go find the actual rule about ties at some point (teach me to ask

> to make a tie for first worth more than a loss (i.e. if you split a table 2/2,
> you have preference over someone who who doesn't, but the VPs might make it
> work that way anyways), but I don't think it is gonna be that important.

Since trying to make sure people to "play to win" (rather than "play
to split the table") was one of the goals of the new scoring system,
I'm not sure that making ties worth something would be a good thing.
:-)

> Yup. Where I see this being problematic, however, is in the obvious
> situation--a guy who accidentally wins one table with a 2-1-1-1 point split but
> gets no other VPs during the rest of the tournament will get into the finals
> way before the guy who never actually wins a table, but gets 2 VPs in each
> round (point splitting each table 3-2). Guy A has 2 VPs where guy B has 6, but
> guy A gets into the finals before guy B, which is kind of wonky. I guess it no
> longer pays to play an intercept deck.

Well, from another point of view it was kinda wonky that guy B
would beat guy A into the finals, considering that guy B never
won a single game in the preliminary rounds. (given that winning
is defined in the rulebook to be "getting more VPs than anyone
else in the game.")

In practice, I suspect that it's very rare for anyone to make
it to the finals by getting 2 VPs per game but never winning
a game. I looked at what the results at the last tournament
I ran would've been under the game-win system, and the only
difference was that the second and third seed going into the
finals would've been reversed (third seed had two table wins
to second seed's one, but fewer VPs). There were several games
where a table win was not awarded (2/2/0/0 splits on 4-player
tables, or 1.5/1.5/.5/0/0 splits on 5-player tables), but that's
probably not a problem.

I think it may pay more to play an intercept deck (that can win
games) than it did before: at a medium-size tournament, you may
only need to win one game (of three) to make the finals, as long
as you get a couple more VPs in your other games. Under the old
system, an intercept deck probably needed two VPs in each of
three games to qualify. Now, if you can manage 3/1/1/0/0 once,
you're doing well, or 2/1/1/1/0, or even 2/1/1/0 on a four-player
table, which is probably much easier to manage. (With a mostly-
focused-backwards intercept deck, you probably get your predator
ousted first. In a five-player game, your initial prey, with a
mostly-free hand, would be liable to oust your grandprey before
your new predator gets killed and then get to mop up that new
predator for 2 VPs; in a four-player game, your new predator *is*
your grandprey, so it should be easier to give 1 VP to each of
two people and keep the last two for yourself.

In theory, anyway.

Josh

In fact, I agree with what you're saying to Peter. But I would
caution anyone to take anything from looking at the results of
tournaments being played under current rules. The fact is, players
may very well (in fact I expect them to) play somewhat differently
with the knowledge that they need game wins to make the finals. So
just going through and recalculating the results given new rules
does not accurately reflect how the rule change will affect
tournaments. Personally, I expect it affect metagame choices and
deck construction at least somewhat and the actual play of the games
significantly.

Fred

It is not more easily said than done. It is *AS* easily said as done.
Speaking in computerese psuedo-code:

If (action === undirected) then
don't do it.

Not a hard concept to program at all. The answer to your question is that
if your deck depends on taking undirected actions, such as voting, you simply
don't do them. Period. You sit there, discarding once per turn if there's
any hope of drawing something that may help you. Or doing nothing at all if
not. Your predator sits there and waits, fruitlessly - at least as far as you're
concerned. If your grandpredator has some kind hope of attacking your predator -
either by extreme enough stealth or by having better combat - they duke it out
and you hope that the latter's position gets beat up enough so that he either
goes away at some point or can't afford to worry about you any more. If your
grandpredator can do neither, then hopefully he's smart enough to do the same
thing as you: nothing. Then whatever else happens in the game that is not to
your liking is not likely going to be to your predator's liking either. This
whole do-nothing strategy may not help, but it can't hurt either. Certainly
there's never a reason to helplessly send your minions off to the slaughter
voluntarily.

That gives too much incentive to split the table between two players.
The whole point of the "game wins" system is make players work for a
win and _not_ settle for a tie.

> >How do you propose to deal with combat deck table-splitting under such a
> >system? This system is really quite delicate about handling such.
>
> By that do you mean 2 combat decks 'agreeing' to share the win by
> beating down everyone else?
>

That's too much. While I agree that people who wind up splitting a
table 2-2 or 2-2-1 (as appropriate) against their will are probably
unduly penalized by this system, giving them half a win doesn't work
either for the reason stated above.

> My guess would be that at the 11th hour, 1 of
> them will break the deal and go for the win.

I think it's been very well established that that seldom happens in
tournament play. There's no incentive to do so. Break a deal like that
once or twice and you get a reputation for doing so in your local area.
You may gain the extra half a win, you may even make the finals of that
tournament where you would not have otherwise but you'll never be able
to deal with most of the people thereabouts ever again. Few players
find this to be a good tradeoff. So it almost never happens. Which is
how we got to the existing state of affairs: too many games being
decided by having two players agree to divide the table.

Fred

8-player tournament. 3 rounds.

If that's what you're looking for, then you'd probably want to advocate something
like granting something like a quarter of a game win or a fifth of a game win for
a tie. Something that's not going to amount to "two ties = one win", because
that's rewarding table-splitting pretty much as completely as the victory point
system does. It's just a little more tricky to arrange since you have to exactly
tie the game instead of, say, splitting the table 3-2. And the trickiness isn't
good either way - the main effect of that issue is to make the result more capricious
rather than either encouraging or discouraging table-splitting.

> >That's your opinion. Anyone who agrees need not care whether they're honored
> >or not because they would consider such agreements worthless. Therefore, the
> >only people who make them are those who assume they'll be honored. And they

> which point we would contest for the win. If he didn't seem willing
> to do that, I might have to hide my intention at that point and 'make
> the deal'.

That kind of deal is not the issue here, IMO. Usually it doesn't come up
because it's not nearly as powerful as the kind of deal that purports to settle
the entire game, including who is the last player standing, at the time it's
made. What you're talking about is inherently much more unstable because
a player offered that deal will figure the player offering it has some means
of pulling the game out when there's only two players left, so it isn't very
valuable to him - at least, not when the game win system is in place, making
any VPs gained in the process much less valuable. So the only way the player
who is offered the deal will take it is if he has a way to pull the game out
when it's down to two players that isn't apparent to his prospective ally.
Knowing that, it becomes very risky to offer such a deal: it will only be
accepted if the other player is likely to be holding the winning hand somehow
that isn't obvious.

All in all, I don't worry a deal that isn't offered to bloody end. If two
players feel like they can gain something by cooperating to oust another
player or players, that's just fine. As long as they have to fight it out
eventually. It's the half-reward for splitting tables that's too easy to
pull off for too much reward (currently) and screws up the dynamics of the
game too much. And the punishment for not keeping deals - that you won't
be able to engage in very successful practice of table-splitting in the
future - is too high a price for most players to feel comfortable paying
just to win one game instead of splitting the table.

> I keep 99% of my deals. For those odd 1% where it might mean the game

Because your assumption is wrong. The point of the deal - and what a lot of people
including myself intensely dislike about it - is that it allows two players who would
normally not be strong enough to easily oust the others to do so.

I don't know what the situation was. Based on your many confusing responses
in this thread, I suspect you don't really understand the point I've been
trying to make. I further suspect this is likely because in your tournament
environment, people have not really discovered the power of negotiating for
a table split.

> >Did you ever think the reason you might be getting so few offers to split
> >games ("odd 1%") is that you won't keep them? It seems pretty logical to
> >me that if you'd never keep them nor ever offer them to other players, that's
> >probably why you never get an opportunities to enter into them.
> >
>
> You're extrapolating here incorrectly. I said I dont see that kind of
> deal.

Exactly. And I think that explains most of our dispute. You don't seem to
believe that such deals can be extremely powerful and difficult to stop. The
only real counterstrategy is frequently to make one's own deals whenever one
has the chance. This is a case where a game strategy - instead of a card -
has become imbalanced. Refusing to participate or honor such deals does
nothing to stop others from engaging in them and being very successful with
them. Only a change in tournament rules fixes the problem.

> >If you're talking about minor deals to temporarily cooperate, those I might
> >make with you. But I think you're overestimating the value of them in
> >comparison to game-ending deals. Play in some of the major tournaments I've
> >played in and they're far, FAR more common than any "1%" figure you're
> >quoting.
>
> By 1% I refer to tablesplitting deals where one player would better
> benefit by breaking the deal.

In any tablesplitting deal (or almost any one except in extremely rare instances,
as far as I know), one player would better benefit by breaking the deal. The whole
basis of such deals is to allow one player to collect two or three points and then
take a dive, granting the other player the last two. If player taking the dive
doesn't honor the deal, he's better off unless he simply fails to survive anyway.

> > You don't seem to be very aware of just how effective they are
> >for getting players into the finals or you wouldn't say a thing like that.
> >
>
> Perhaps so. As i've said, I havnt seen that myself. Seeing as that
> would appear to be an out of game consideration, how are players
> ethically doing this?

Ethics doesn't enter into it. Any legal means of winning a tournament is ethical,
unless you're bending the spirit of the rules or something along those lines. I
don't really want open that can of worms.

I think you meant to ask, "Why is it legal in view of the 'out-of-game consideration'
rule." The answer is that even by this rule, players are allowed to settle for fewer
than the number of victory points needed for a win if they can argue that that would
represent the best they can possibly do at this point in the game. In short, "I can't
hope to get three victory points given my game position, so therefore it's legal to
settle for a deal that allows me two victory points." In my experience, such a claim
seems frequently to be extremely questionable, but I do care to call a judge over and
argue about it. Nor have I ever seen anyone else do it. In practice, the out-of-game
consideration rule just isn't effective at stopping this. That's why we need the 'game
win' tournament rule, and we need it to have teeth even if it screws people who wound
up in a genuine (and unfortunate) two-two VP split.

Fred
